candidate.answerReason: The whole-dollar full price must be a divisor of 4002 between 15 and 28, so it is 23. There are 34 full-price tickets, raising $782, which matches choice A.

methods.label: Bound the whole-dollar price
methods.explanation:
The whole-dollar condition lets us restrict the full price using divisibility. Let \(p\) be the positive integer full price in dollars, and let \(n\) be the number of full-price tickets. The other \(140-n\) tickets cost \(p/2\) dollars each, so
\[
pn+\frac p2(140-n)=2001.
\]
Multiplying by \(2\) and collecting factors gives
\[
p(140+n)=4002.
\]
In particular, \(p\) divides \(4002\).

Every ticket costs between \(p/2\) and \(p\), so
\[
70p\le2001\le140p.
\]
Because \(p\) is an integer, these bounds give \(15\le p\le28\). Now
\[
4002=2\cdot3\cdot23\cdot29.
\]
A divisor in the required range cannot contain the factor \(29\). A divisor using neither \(23\) nor \(29\) is at most \(2\cdot3=6\), while the only multiple of \(23\) between \(15\) and \(28\) is \(23\). Hence \(p=23\).

It follows that \(140+n=4002/23=174\), so \(n=34\). The full-price tickets raise
\[
23\cdot34=\boxed{782}\text{ dollars}.
\]
The remaining \(106\) tickets raise \(106\cdot11.50=1219\) dollars, and \(782+1219=2001\), confirming the conditions. The answer is choice \(\mathrm{A}\).
